mainInsight: After sorting, if nums[l] + nums[r] is below the (adjusted) target then every index between l and r also works with l, so add r - l at once and advance l; otherwise shrink r.

promptVariants: Why does `count += r - l` count several triplets at once?
Justify adding r - l when nums[l] + nums[r] < target.
cards.answer: The array is sorted, so for the fixed l every index between l+1 and r has value <= nums[r]; each such pair (l, m) also sums below the target. That is exactly r - l valid pairs, after which l can advance.
keyPoints: Sorted => values between l and r are <= nums[r]
r - l pairs with this l
cards.explanation: Counting a range instead of one match is the key difference from 3Sum.

promptVariants: Why is target reduced by nums[idx] inside the helper, and why start l at idx + 1?
cards.answer: Fixing nums[idx] turns the problem into counting pairs after it whose sum is below target - nums[idx]. Starting at idx + 1 ensures i < j < k so each triplet is counted once. It returns the number of qualifying pairs for that i.
cards.explanation: Note the stated return type list[list[int]] is wrong; it returns an int.

cards.answer: Only the multiset of values matters for the sum, so sorting preserves the count
cards.explanation: Any triplet of indices maps to a triplet of values; reordering the array merely relabels indices, so the number of qualifying triplets is unchanged.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Sorting changes the answer, so the count: It does not change the count.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Only for arrays whose values are all dis: Duplicates are counted per index triplet and still work.
